exercises.video_explanation_script: The barbell bench press is the king of chest exercises. Lie on the bench with your eyes under the bar and your feet flat on the ground. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Unrack the bar and hold it over your chest with arms extended. Pull your shoulder blades together and down - this position is crucial. From here, lower the bar under control to your lower chest, keeping your elbows tucked at about 45 degrees from your body. Touch the bar to your chest lightly, then drive it back up explosively. The bar path should be slightly diagonal - up and slightly back toward your face. The bench press builds incredible chest strength and mass when performed correctly.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The incline barbell bench press is essential for developing your upper chest. Set the bench to a 30 to 45-degree incline. Lie back on the bench with your feet flat on the ground and pull your shoulder blades together. Unrack the bar and hold it over your upper chest. From here, lower the bar to your upper chest or clavicle area - higher than where you'd touch on flat bench. Keep your elbows tucked at about 45 degrees. Then press the bar straight up until your arms are fully extended. The incline angle shifts emphasis to your upper pecs, which is crucial for a full, well-developed chest. Most people can handle about 70-85% of their flat bench weight on incline.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The dumbbell bench press is fantastic for chest development. To get into position, sit on the edge of the bench with the dumbbells on your thighs. Lie back while bringing the dumbbells up to chest level. Start with your arms extended and dumbbells above your chest. From here, lower the dumbbells down to the sides of your chest, going deeper than you could with a barbell. Keep your elbows at about 45 degrees. Feel that deep stretch in your chest. Then press the dumbbells back up, bringing them together slightly at the top and squeezing your chest. Dumbbells allow for greater range of motion and require more stabilization than barbells, making them excellent for building chest mass and addressing imbalances.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The incline dumbbell press is one of the best exercises for building your upper chest. Set the bench to a 30 to 45-degree incline. Get the dumbbells into position by sitting with them on your thighs, then lying back as you bring them to shoulder level. Start with the dumbbells extended above your upper chest. Lower them down to the sides of your shoulders and upper chest, keeping your elbows at about 45 degrees. Go deep to get a full stretch in your upper pecs. Then press them back up, bringing them slightly together at the top and squeezing your upper chest. The incline dumbbell press gives you greater range of motion than the barbell version and is excellent for building that full, well-developed upper chest.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The dumbbell fly is a classic chest isolation exercise. Lie on a flat bench with dumbbells held together above your chest, palms facing each other. Maintain a slight bend in your elbows - this angle stays the same throughout the entire movement. From here, open your arms out to the sides in a wide arc, like you're hugging a large barrel. Lower until the dumbbells are about level with your shoulders and you feel a deep stretch across your chest. Then squeeze your chest to bring the dumbbells back together above your chest in that same arc motion. Think about your elbows coming together, not your hands. The dumbbell fly is all about the chest stretch and squeeze - use lighter weight than pressing and focus on feeling your chest work.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The push-up is a fundamental exercise for chest development. Start in a high plank position with your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width and your body in a completely straight line from head to heels. From here, lower your chest toward the ground by bending your elbows, keeping them at about 45 degrees from your body. Your entire body should move as one rigid unit - don't let your hips sag or pike up. Lower until your chest touches or nearly touches the ground, then push yourself back up to full arm extension. Squeeze your glutes and core throughout to maintain that straight body position. The push-up is one of the best bodyweight chest exercises and can be progressed indefinitely with variations.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The cable fly is fantastic for chest isolation because cables provide constant tension throughout the movement. Set the pulleys at about chest height and stand in the middle with a staggered stance. Lean forward slightly from your hips. Grab the handles with your arms extended out to your sides and a slight bend in your elbows. This elbow angle stays the same throughout. From here, squeeze your chest to bring the handles together in front of you in a big arc motion, like you're hugging someone. Really squeeze your chest when the handles meet - even cross your hands slightly. Then control the handles as they open back out to the sides. The constant tension from the cables makes this excellent for that peak contraction and for really feeling your chest work.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The chest dip is one of the best exercises for building your lower chest. The key to making dips a chest exercise instead of a tricep exercise is the forward lean. Grab the parallel bars and press yourself up to the starting position. From here, lean your torso forward about 10 to 30 degrees - the more you lean, the more chest you'll use. Lower yourself down by bending your elbows until your upper arms are about parallel to the ground. Feel the stretch in your lower chest. Then push yourself back up, maintaining that forward lean. Squeeze your chest at the top. If you can't do bodyweight dips yet, use a band or machine for assistance. Once you master bodyweight dips, add weight with a belt or vest.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The decline barbell bench press targets your lower chest. Set the bench to a 15 to 30-degree decline and secure your feet in the ankle pads. Lie back on the bench with your eyes under the bar. Unrack the bar and hold it over your lower chest with your arms extended. Lower the bar to your lower chest or sternum area - lower than where you'd touch on flat bench. Keep your elbows at about 45 degrees. Then press the bar back up to full extension. The decline angle shifts emphasis to your lower pecs and many people find they can handle more weight on decline than flat bench. Always use a spotter on decline bench - it's harder to bail safely than flat bench.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The incline dumbbell fly is perfect for isolating your upper chest. Set the bench to a 30 to 45-degree incline. Get the dumbbells into position and start with them held together above your upper chest, palms facing each other. Maintain a slight bend in your elbows - this angle stays the same throughout. From here, open your arms out to the sides in a wide arc until the dumbbells are about level with your shoulders. Feel the deep stretch across your upper chest. Then squeeze your upper chest to bring the dumbbells back together above you. The incline angle specifically targets your upper pecs, and the fly motion provides that crucial stretch and contraction that builds the mind-muscle connection. This is essential for complete chest development.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The machine chest press is a safe and effective way to build chest strength. Adjust the seat so the handles are at about mid-chest level. Sit with your back firmly against the pad and your feet flat on the ground. Grasp the handles at chest level. From here, push the handles forward by pressing through your chest until your arms are fully extended. Squeeze your chest at the end. Then control the weight as it returns to the starting position. The machine provides stability so you can focus purely on working your chest, and you can safely train to failure. The chest press machine is excellent for beginners learning the pressing pattern and for advanced lifters wanting to load heavy without worrying about balance.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The high-to-low cable crossover is excellent for targeting your lower chest. Set the pulleys at the highest position and stand in the middle with a staggered stance. Lean forward slightly from your hips. Grab the handles with your arms extended up and out to your sides with a slight bend in your elbows. From here, squeeze your lower chest to bring the handles down and together in front of you. The motion is downward and inward - aim for your hands to cross in front of your thighs. Really squeeze your lower chest at the bottom. Then control the handles as they return up and out. The downward angle from high cables emphasizes your lower chest, and the cables provide constant tension throughout the movement. This is perfect for finishing off your chest workout and getting that lower chest pump.
